newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Krupp says Buba cannot ignore weak economy.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Krupp says Buba cannot ignore weak economy.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp said on Thursday that record German jobless figures issued last week proved the German economy was in a grave position and that the Bundesbank could not ignore this.

"The jobless figures published last week reminded us once again of our dramatic economic position," Krupp said in a speech to a new year's reception in Hamburg. "Even monetary policy cannot be indifferent to this situation, particularly when it does not need to have any worries about inflation."
Turning to the euro, Krupp said it would be hard for financial markets to attack the euro currency bloc because of its size.
Krupp, who is seen as a dove on the Bundesbank council, is head of the regional central bank based in Hamburg.
Krupp said the launch of the euro would help to reduce some economic problems because a considerable part of trade would then be within a single currency block.
"At the same time, the euro block will be of a size which financial markets will find hard to attack," he said.
Referring to Germany's current domestic problems, Krupp said that monetary policy alone could nonetheless not correct all problems in the economy.
The Bundesbank also had to take account of exchange rate considerations and the impact on long-term interest rates when taking its policy decisions, Krupp said.

Its responsibilty for price stability of Europe's anchor currency, the mark, meant that it could not simply follow an exchange rate driven policy, as many of its European neighbours did with respect to their currencies' level against the mark.
The central bank also had to study carefully the likely impact of any rate moves on capital markets, as long-term rates were also of considerable importance for the economy.
However Krupp added that wage policy and monetary policy had already made considerable contributions toward improving the economic environment and criticised fiscal policy for failing to do so.
"Fiscal policy continues to send out signals which are not just restrictive, but above all hold a considerable uncertainty," he said.
